Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.
Under the measure of [[thm-countable-product-of-probability-spaces]], the coordinate maps $X_n(x)=x_n$ have laws $\mu_n$ and are independent.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. Then the following are
equivalent:

1. the family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent;
2. for every natural number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices
   $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and every choice of measurable sets
   $B_k\in\Sigma_{i_k}$,
   $$\mathbb P\bigl(X_{i_0}\in B_0,\dots,X_{i_{n-1}}\in B_{n-1}\bigr)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(X_{i_k}\in B_k).$$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

For measurable spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$, put
$E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i$. For finite $F\subseteq I$, let
$\pi_F:E\to\prod_{i\in F}E_i$ be restriction to $F$ (the singleton empty
product when $F=\varnothing$). On $\prod_{i\in F}E_i$, write $q_i$ for the
$i$th coordinate map and define

$$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i:=\sigma\{q_i^{-1}(A):i\in F,\ A\in\mathcal E_i\}.$$

For $F=\varnothing$ this is the two-set sigma-algebra on the singleton. If
$e:[n]\to F$ is any enumeration, coordinate relabelling identifies this
sigma-algebra with the recursively defined finite product sigma-algebra of
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: both are
generated by the same coordinate inverse images. Thus the notation is
independent of the enumeration.

A **finite-coordinate cylinder** is $\pi_F^{-1}(A)$ for
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The **cylinder sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal C_I:=\sigma\{\pi_F^{-1}(A):F\subseteq I\text{ finite},\ A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i\}.$$

This is the product sigma-algebra on the arbitrary product; the empty-support cylinder is either $\varnothing$ or $E$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$. In the product topology on $\mathbb R^n$,
each of the following families generates $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)$: all open
sets; all closed sets; all compact sets; all Euclidean open balls; all open
boxes; all rational open boxes; and all rational half-open boxes
$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ with rational endpoints $a_i<b_i$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: By [F1], every specified pattern on $n$ distinct coordinates has probability $2^{-n}$. Thus $K_{s,n}$ is uniform on $\{0,\ldots,2^n-1\}$. The events that the first $m$ bits after position $n$ are all zero, or all one, decrease to the corresponding constant-tail events and have probabilities $2^{-m}$. By [F4], both constant-tail events have probability zero. The partial sums defining each $U_s$ are measurable and increase to $U_s$ by [F6].

Fix a dyadic threshold $t=k2^{-n}$ with $0\le k\le2^n$. If $K_{s,n}<k$, then $U_s\le t$; if $K_{s,n}>k$, then $U_s>t$; if $K_{s,n}=k$, then $U_s\le t$ only on the null event $T_{s,n}=0$. Hence $\mathbb P(U_s\le k2^{-n})=k2^{-n}$. For an arbitrary $t\in[0,1]$, dyadic lower and upper approximations differ by at most $2^{-n}$, so monotonicity of the CDF and passage to the limit give $\mathbb P(U_s\le t)=t$. Outside $[0,1]$ the CDF is $0$ or $1$.

For finitely many streams and dyadic thresholds $t_s=k_s2^{-n}$, the joint event $\bigcap_s\{U_s\le t_s\}$ differs by a null set from the event that every prefix integer $K_{s,n}<k_s$. Pairwise disjointness makes all prefix coordinates distinct. By [F2] these coordinate bits are independent and by [F1] each is fair, so the probability that each stream's prefix integer is below $k_s$ is the product $\prod_s(k_s2^{-n})$.

For arbitrary thresholds $t_s\in[0,1]$, dyadic lower and upper approximations squeeze the joint probability between products converging to $\prod_s t_s$. Thus the joint CDF equals the product-uniform CDF. The lower rectangles $\prod_s[0,t_s]$, including the whole cube, are closed under intersections. They generate each coordinate slab $\{x:x_s\le t\}$ by taking the other thresholds to be $1$; complements and finite intersections then give the intersections of the cube with all rational half-open boxes (thresholds outside $[0,1]$ give empty or full slabs). By [F7] these generate the relative Borel sigma-algebra of the cube. Both laws have total mass one there, a finite-measure exhaustion. Thus [F5] identifies the joint law with the product-uniform law. In particular every Borel rectangle has the product of its marginal probabilities, so the rectangle criterion [F3] gives independence of the generated sigma-algebras.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

1. Let $X$ be a real random variable, let $\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let
   $F_X(x)=\mathbb P(X\le x)$. Then $F_X$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous,
   satisfies
   $$\lim_{x\to-\infty}F_X(x)=0,\qquad \lim_{x\to+\infty}F_X(x)=1,$$
   and obeys
   $$\mathbb P_X((a,b])=F_X(b)-F_X(a)\qquad(a<b).$$
2. Conversely, if $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is nondecreasing and
   right-continuous with
   $$\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0,\qquad \lim_{x\to+\infty}F(x)=1,$$
   then there is a unique Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$ such
   that
   $$\mu((a,b])=F(b)-F(a)\qquad(a<b),$$
   equivalently
   $$F(x)=\mu((-\infty,x])\qquad(x\in\mathbb R).$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. **Degenerate boxes.** If $a_i \le b_i$ are reals with $a_{i_0} = b_{i_0}$ for
   some $i_0 < n$, then every set $R$ between the open box
   $\{x : a_i < x_i < b_i\ (i<n)\}$ and the closed rectangle $[a,b]$ is Lebesgue
   measurable with $\lambda_n(R) = 0$.
2. **Coordinate hyperplanes.** For $i_0 < n$ and a real $c$, the set
   $$H_{i_0,c} \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_{i_0} = c \,\}$$
   is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(H_{i_0,c}) = 0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,

$$B_{s,k}(\omega)=\omega_{j_{s,k}},\qquad U_s(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}B_{s,k}(\omega)2^{-k}.$$
Then each $U_s$ has the uniform Borel law on $[0,1]$, and the family $(U_s)$ is independent. No other choice principle is used.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $w\ge2$, $M=2^w$, integers $a,c$, and a seed $x_0\in\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ be inputs. For an integer $r$, $[r]_M$ denotes the unique residue in $\{0,\ldots,M-1\}$ congruent to $r$ modulo $M$. The state sequence and returned midpoint word are
$$x_{n+1}=[ax_n+c]_M,\qquad u_n=\frac{x_n+1/2}{M}\quad(n\ge0).$$
The output is the deterministic state sequence, or its midpoint conversion $u_n\in(0,1)$. A full-period LCG is the special case $a\equiv1\pmod4$ and $c$ odd; its period is proved separately. A seed chosen at random is a distinct probability model, not part of this deterministic procedure.

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty finite set. Its **uniform probability space** assigns every $\omega\in\Omega$ the weight $1/|\Omega|$. Thus every event $A\subseteq\Omega$ has
$$\mathbb P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}.$$
Nonemptiness is required so that the denominator is positive.

Finite products are taken in the commutative monoid $(\mathbb{Z},\cdot,1)$ of
[[lem-units-of-z]] as in [[def-monoid-finite-product]], and a **list of primes
of length $r$** is a function $p : r \to \mathbb{Z}$ on the von Neumann natural
$r = \{0,\dots,r-1\}$ with every $p_i$ prime ([[def-prime]]).

1. **Existence.** Every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $n \ge 1$ is $\prod_{i<r} p_i$
   for some $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and some list $p$ of primes of length $r$
   ([[thm-prime-factorisation-exists]]).
2. **Uniqueness up to order.** Let $p$ and $q$ be lists of primes, of lengths
   $r$ and $s$. If

   $$\prod_{i<r} p_i \;=\; \prod_{j<s} q_j ,$$

   then $r = s$, and there is a permutation $\pi \in \operatorname{Sym}(r)$
   ([[def-symmetric-group]]) with

   $$q_i \;=\; p_{\pi(i)} \qquad \text{for every } i < r .$$

At $r = 0$ clause 2 says that the only list of primes whose product is $1$ is the
empty list, and the permutation condition is vacuous.

Let $p \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-integers]]), ordered as in [[def-int-order]], with
divisibility as in [[def-divides-in-z]]. Then $p$ is **prime** when

$$p > 1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad d \mid p \ \text{ with } \ d > 0 \ \text{ force } \ d = 1 \ \text{ or } \ d = p .$$

In words: $p$ exceeds $1$, and its only positive divisors are $1$ and $p$. An
integer $n$ with $n > 1$ that is not prime is **composite**; unfolding the
definition, $n$ is composite exactly when $n > 1$ and $n$ has a positive divisor
$d$ with $d \ne 1$ and $d \ne n$.

**Numerals.** For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ the symbol $k$ inside $\mathbb{Z}$ means
$\iota(k)$, the embedding of [[lem-nat-embeds-int]]; in particular $0$ and $1$
are the ring constants of [[def-int-operations]].

**Boundary values, stated rather than assumed.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]) and $\mathbb{Z}$ contains $0$, $1$ and the negatives,
so the small cases are recorded explicitly. The clause $p > 1$ decides all of
them at once:

- $1$ is **not** prime, since $1 > 1$ is false, and not composite either, since
  composite also requires $n > 1$.
- $0$ is **not** prime, since $0 > 1$ is false. This is decided by the size
  clause alone and not by counting divisors: every integer divides $0$
  ([[def-divides-in-z]]), so the divisor condition is not what rules $0$ out.
- Every negative integer is neither prime nor composite, again because $p > 1$
  fails. So a prime is in particular positive, and $-2$, $-3$, $-5$ are not
  primes in this library, though each is $-1$ times one.

Thus "prime" and "composite" between them classify exactly the integers greater
than $1$, and nothing else.

**The same condition read over all divisors.** For $p > 1$ the following are
equivalent:

1. the only positive divisors of $p$ are $1$ and $p$;
2. the only divisors of $p$ are $1$, $-1$, $p$ and $-p$.

That 2 implies 1 is immediate, since of those four only $1$ and $p$ are positive
($p > 1 > 0$, so $-1 < 0$ and $-p < 0$). For the converse let $d \mid p$. Since
$p > 1$ we have $p \ne 0$, so $d \ne 0$ by [[lem-divisor-bound]]; and
$|d| \mid p$, because $|d|$ is $d$ or $-d$ ([[def-int-abs]]) and those two divide
$p$ together ([[lem-divisibility-basic]]). Also $|d| \ge 0$ and $|d| \ne 0$
([[lem-int-abs-properties]]), so $|d| > 0$ and clause 1 gives $|d| = 1$ or
$|d| = p$. If $|d| = 1$ then $d = 1$ or $d = -1$, by the case split defining
$|d|$; and if $|d| = p = |p|$ then $d = up$ for a unit $u \in \{1,-1\}$
([[lem-associates-characterisation]], [[lem-units-of-z]]), that is $d = p$ or
$d = -p$. Both readings are used below without further comment.

**Why $1$ is excluded, and it is not a matter of taste.** The exclusion is
forced by the uniqueness half of [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-arithmetic]],
proved on this page: if $1$ counted as a prime, a factorisation could be padded
with any number of factors $1$, so lists of different lengths would represent
the same integer and no permutation could match them. Existence of a
factorisation would survive the change; it is uniqueness alone that fixes the
convention, and the explicit witness is recorded on the companion page.

derivations.claim: For $m\ge1$, let $S_m=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a^j$. Induction on $m$ in the affine recurrence gives $x_m\equiv a^m x_0+cS_m\pmod{2^w}$, and the same formula holds from any starting state.

For every $k\ge0$, $a^{2^k}\equiv1\pmod{2^{k+2}}$. The base case is $a\equiv1\pmod4$. If $a^{2^k}=1+q2^{k+2}$, then squaring gives $a^{2^{k+1}}=1+q2^{k+3}+q^2 2^{2k+4}$, whose difference from $1$ is divisible by $2^{k+3}$.
Write $S_{2^k}=2^k q_k$. For $k=0$, $q_0=1$ is odd. The identity $S_{2^{k+1}}=S_{2^k}(1+a^{2^k})$ and $a^{2^k}\equiv1\pmod4$ show that $(1+a^{2^k})/2$ is odd; hence $q_{k+1}=q_k(1+a^{2^k})/2$ is odd.

For every $0\le k<w$, the affine iterate in step 1.1 and facts from steps 2.1 and 3.1 give $x_{2^k}-x_0\equiv(a^{2^k}-1)x_0+cS_{2^k}\equiv 2^k\pmod{2^{k+1}}$. Indeed, the first summand is divisible by $2^{k+2}$, while $S_{2^k}=2^kq_k$ with $q_k$ odd and $c$ odd; thus a return at $2^k$ is impossible modulo $2^{k+1}$.

Taking $k=w$ in the affine iterate from step 1.1 shows $x_{2^w}\equiv x_0\pmod{2^w}$: the first summand $(a^{2^w}-1)x_0$ is divisible by $2^{w+2}$ and $cS_{2^w}$ by $2^w$. Thus a least positive return time $d$ exists.

This least return time divides $2^w$. Indeed, write $2^w=qd+r$ with $0\le r<d$. Determinism and $x_d=x_0$ imply $x_{n+d}=x_n$ for all $n\ge0$, so $x_{2^w}=x_r$. Since $x_{2^w}=x_0$, minimality of $d$ forces $r=0$, hence $2^w=dh$ for some positive integer $h$. By [F3], factor $d$ and $h$ into primes; their combined list is a prime factorization of $2^w$, whose prime list consists of $w$ copies of 2. Uniqueness in [F3] implies every prime factor of $d$ is 2, so $d=2^j$ for some $0\le j\le w$. If $j<w$, step 4.1 shows $x_{2^j}\ne x_0$ modulo $2^{j+1}$ and therefore modulo $2^w$, contradiction. Hence $d=2^w$, for every seed.

The map $x\mapsto[ax+c]_{2^w}$ is a permutation because $a$ is odd: if two outputs agree then $a(x-y)$ is divisible by $2^w$, and oddness makes $a$ invertible modulo $2^w$. By [F2], a uniform seed therefore remains uniform at every time. The adjacent-pair law is supported on exactly the $2^w$ pairs $(x,[ax+c]_{2^w})$, while the product of two uniform marginals assigns positive mass to all $2^{2w}$ pairs. Since $w\ge2$, $2^w<2^{2w}$, so the adjacent states are dependent.

2. Otherwise return the word $\pi_k(c)$ and replace $c$ by $c+1$.

A fixed key and counter interval define a deterministic stream. Any random-key model or computational pseudorandomness guarantee must be stated separately.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ carry the countable product probability measure of fair bits. For any finite family of pairwise disjoint infinite coordinate sequences $j_{s,1},j_{s,2},\ldots$, define
$$B_{s,k}(\omega)=\omega_{j_{s,k}},\qquad U_s(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}B_{s,k}(\omega)2^{-k}.$$
Then each $U_s$ has the uniform Borel law on $[0,1]$, and the family $(U_s)$ is independent. No other choice principle is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(U,V)$ have product Lebesgue probability law on $(0,1)^2$, and set
$$R=\sqrt{-2\log U},\quad \Theta=2\pi V,\quad Z=(R\cos\Theta,R\sin\Theta).$$
Then $Z$ has the Borel density
$$g(x,y)=\frac1{2\pi}e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}=\phi(x)\phi(y),\qquad \phi(t)=\frac{e^{-t^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}.$$
In particular, its coordinates are independent with density $\phi$. Also $\mathbb P(R>r)=e^{-r^2/2}$ for $r\ge0$ and $\mathbb E R^2=2$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Initially $F(\ell)\le u\le F(r)$ by the algorithm's bracket test. If $F(m)\le u$, replacing $\ell$ by $m$ preserves both inequalities by monotonicity; if $F(m)>u$, replacing $r$ by $m$ preserves them. After $N$ steps, $r-\ell=(b-a)2^{-N}$, so the modulus certificate gives $F(r)-F(\ell)\le\varepsilon$. Since $\widehat x\in[\ell,r]$, monotonicity puts both $F(\widehat x)$ and $u$ in this range, proving $|F(\widehat x)-u|\le\varepsilon$. For a continuous $F$, uniform continuity [F3] supplies a positive distance tolerance; since $(b-a)2^{-N}\to0$ by [F4], some finite $N$ meets it. A successful run evaluates the two endpoints once and one midpoint per update, hence uses $N+2$ CDF evaluations; the budget explicitly includes these endpoints.

For fixed depth $N$, the grid consists of the $2^N$ cells in the partition of $[a,b]$; their left endpoints are $a+j(b-a)2^{-N}$ for $0\le j<2^N$. At each bisection, the tested midpoint separates the remaining candidate left endpoints into lower and upper halves, and the rule keeps the upper half exactly when $\widetilde F(m)\le u$. Induction on the $N$ updates shows that the final $\ell$ is the greatest such left endpoint and $r$ is the next grid point. As $u$ increases, the predicate set can only grow, so the selected cell midpoint $g(u)$ is nondecreasing.

Since $Q(u)\in[a,b]$, [A4] implies $|F(\widehat x)-F(Q(u))|\ge m|\widehat x-Q(u)|$. By [F1], $Q(u)\le Q(u)$ implies $u\le F(Q(u))$. For every $y<Q(u)$, the reverse implication in [F1] gives $F(y)<u$; taking $y\uparrow Q(u)$ and using [A3] gives $F(Q(u))\le u$. Thus $F(Q(u))=u$, and step 1.1 yields $m|\widehat x-Q(u)|\le\varepsilon$.

Fix $x$ and set $E=\{u\in[0,1]:g(u)\le x\}$ and $t=\sup(E\cup\{0\})$. Monotonicity makes $E$ an initial interval. If $u<t$, then $u\in E$, so $\widetilde F(x)\ge\widetilde F(g(u))\ge u-\varepsilon$. If $u>t$, then $u\notin E$, so $g(u)>x$ and $\widetilde F(x)\le\widetilde F(g(u))\le u+\varepsilon$. Taking one-sided limits gives $|\widetilde F(x)-t|\le\varepsilon$; if $t=0$ or $1$, the missing side follows from $0\le\widetilde F(x)\le1$. The set $E$ is either an initial closed or open interval, or empty/all; its $q$-bit midpoint-grid probability differs from $t$ by at most $\delta_q$, using the strict or non-strict CDF bound in [F2]. Thus $d_K(\mathcal L(g(U_q)),\widetilde F)\le\delta_q+\varepsilon$.
The uniform CDF error implies $d_K(\widetilde F,F)\le\eta$. The triangle inequality for the supremum norm of CDF differences and step 2.2 give the stated $\delta_q+\varepsilon+\eta$ bound.

$$R=\sqrt{-2\log U},\quad \Theta=2\pi V,\quad Z=(R\cos\Theta,R\sin\Theta).$$

$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or

Input an integer bit budget $b\ge1$, two disjoint ideal fair-bit subsequences as in
[[thm-independent-fair-bit-streams-produce-uniforms]], and a fixed deterministic
configuration consisting of finite dyadic format parameters, positive integer
series truncation indices $N\ge1$ and nonnegative integer total split budgets
$B\ge0$ for the log/root interval evaluators, positive dyadic log/root width
targets, and phase parameters $0<\tau\le1/4$, integer exponent limits
$e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$, integer precisions $2\le p_0\le p_{\max}$,
and a positive integer elementary-series cap $J\ge1$. Every call uses
these fixed parameters; a failed call returns `inconclusive` with its supplier
status. No success at a requested width is promised for arbitrary fixed budgets.
The midpoint convention is [[thm-midpoint-bit-stream-coupling-and-error]], and
the exact reference transform is [[lem-box-muller-product-density-and-radius-moment]].

1. Take the first $b$ bits from each subsequence and form the exact dyadics
   $u_j=(K_j+1/2)2^{-b}$. Enclose $u_1$ by directed dyadic endpoints in the
   selected format. If this is non-finite or its lower endpoint is not
   positive, return `inconclusive`; underflow may not turn a log argument
   into an accepted interval containing zero.

2. Apply [[alg-budgeted-validated-range-evaluation]] to the logarithm DAG on
   that interval with the configured finite parameters and log width target.
   On `certified(L,X)`, write $L=[L_-,L_+]$ and set
   $\widehat\ell=L_-$, $\eta_\ell=L_+-L_-$. The natural logarithm equals
   the integral logarithm by [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]], so
   $L_-\le\log u_1<0$. Compute the exact dyadic $q=-2\widehat\ell\ge0$.

3. Enclose $q$ by directed endpoints in the configured format; reject
   non-finite endpoints or a negative lower endpoint. Apply the same budgeted
   procedure to its square-root DAG with the root width target. On a
   certified interval $S=[S_-,S_+]$, set $\widehat r=S_-$ and
   $\eta_s=S_+-S_-$. The range guarantee of
   [[thm-budgeted-range-evaluation-terminates-and-is-sound]] gives
   $|\widehat\ell-\log u_1|\le\eta_\ell$ and
   $|\widehat r-\sqrt q|\le\eta_s$. Width differences and the products in
   these instructions are exact dyadic arithmetic.

4. Call [[alg-na-certified-unit-circle-phase]] on the exact rational
   $q_{\rm phase}=2u_2$ and configured phase parameters. On its certified
   return $(\widehat w,\epsilon)$, set
   $\widehat t=(\Re\widehat w,\Im\widehat w)$ and $\eta_t=\epsilon$.
   By [[thm-na-certified-unit-circle-phase-enclosure]],
   $\|\widehat t-(\cos(2\pi u_2),\sin(2\pi u_2))\|_2\le\eta_t$,
   including pi, angle, truncation and directed-endpoint errors. This is the
   existing phase routine, with its existing canonical-pi bridge.

   the dyadic certificates $\eta_\ell,\eta_s,\eta_t$. If any preceding

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

For the fixed-depth procedure of [[alg-certified-bracketed-cdf-inversion]], a successful call uses two endpoint evaluations and $N$ midpoint evaluations, at most $N+2$ CDF evaluations in total. For every continuous CDF on its compact bracket, some finite depth meets each positive modulus tolerance. The bracket invariant holds and its returned point satisfies $|F(\widehat x)-u|\le\varepsilon$. For $u\in(0,1)$, if the exact quantile $Q(u)$ lies in $[a,b]$ and a density $f$ satisfies $F(y)-F(x)=\int_x^y f(t)\,dt$ and $f\ge m>0$ almost everywhere on the bracket, then $|\widehat x-Q(u)|\le\varepsilon/m$.

For the distribution bound, assume the procedure is run with one fixed depth and bracket on every $u\in[0,1]$, with $\widetilde F(a)=0$, $\widetilde F(b)=1$, and residual at most $\varepsilon$ for a continuous CDF $\widetilde F$. Let $g(u)$ be its returned point. Then $g$ is nondecreasing. If $\sup_x|F(x)-\widetilde F(x)|\le\eta$ for another CDF $F$, then
$$d_K\bigl(\mathcal L(g(U_q)),F\bigr)\le\delta_q+\varepsilon+\eta,$$
where $U_q$ is the $q$-bit midpoint uniform, $q\ge1$, and $\delta_q=2^{-q-1}$. If the target is unbounded, the finite-bracket algorithm alone has no global distribution guarantee; its outside-bracket status remains tail-unresolved. Here $d_K(\mu,\nu)=\sup_x|F_\mu(x)-F_\nu(x)|$.

If $\widehat x>1$, then $\widehat x^2>1$, contradicting $\varepsilon\le1$; hence $\widehat x\in[0,1]$ and $F(\widehat x)=\widehat x^2=\varepsilon$. Under the stated endpoint convention, the target is $0$, so the residual is $\varepsilon$ while the spatial error is $\sqrt\varepsilon$.

The ratio $\sqrt\varepsilon/\varepsilon=1/\sqrt\varepsilon$ is unbounded as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$: for any $M>0$, take $0<\varepsilon<\min(1,1/(M+1)^2)$, so [F1] gives $\sqrt\varepsilon<1/(M+1)$ by comparing nonnegative squares, and the ratio exceeds $M$. Also $f(x)=2x$ has infimum $0$ on every bracket touching zero. Thus no uniform constant converts CDF residual to spatial error here; the lower-density hypothesis in [F2] is necessary.
